source_read: PDF, pp. 1–7 (all pages): text read in full; Tables 1–2 (p. 4) and Table 3 (p. 5) checked on rendered pages; Table 1 person-period percentages and the Table 3 sample recomputed; online supplement not available.

key_findings.note: p. 3, 3.1: both paragraphs match. The note is right: 293/1,044 = 28.1%; abstract 28%, Methods 2.8 28.2%.

Table 1 (rendered p. 4): 2.51 (1.75, 3.59), 2.93 (2.08, 4.10), 2.11 (1.50, 2.98), 1.53 (1.15, 2.04); at 18–21, 19 (33.9%) of those who used against 67 (7.0%) of those who did not. 3.2 begins on p. 3 and ends on p. 4, as the locator says.
Table 2 (rendered p. 4) and note d; 3.3, 1st–2nd paragraphs.
p. 4, 3.3, 1st paragraph: b = 0.62, se = 0.13, printed as p < .05, stronger in women; no other interaction significant.
Table 3 (rendered p. 5): all twelve odds ratios and intervals match. The note is right; see missed for a further limit of this analysis (exposure and outcome not period-matched).

key_findings.correction: The paper reports 'inconclusive evidence of associations (all p values > 0.05)' for ecstasy after full adjustment (3.5, p. 5), not that ecstasy showed no association. Suggested: 'Ecstasy (MDMA) use, analysed the same way, showed no statistically significant association with any of the four outcomes after full adjustment (all p > 0.05; the authors call the evidence inconclusive); 38.5% of the cohort reported ecstasy use against 28.2% methamphetamine use.' The same fix applies to the card's exposure.polysubstance field ('shows no adjusted association').

reporting_issues.note: Table 3 on the rendered page: victimisation and intimate-partner perpetration both print 1.89 (1.15–3.11) in the monthly column; victimisation 'once or twice' also ends at 3.11. Each interval is symmetric on the log scale, so neither cell is impossible; duplication remains the likelier explanation.
Table 2 note e; no coding of age or sex is given anywhere in the article.

Recomputed from the counts and percentages (person-periods): perpetration 4.5% and 11.3% (printed 11.8 and 26.3); victimisation 5.3% and 12.7% (11.7 and 25.5); intimate-partner perpetration 6.4% and 12.5% (11.3 and 20.9); intimate-partner victimisation 11.2% and 18.2% (11.1 and 18.2).

The facts are right but the place is not: 'once or twice only in any age period' is in Methods 2.2, which is on p. 2 (right column), not p. 3; Results 3.1 (p. 3) says never more than 1–2 times per year; Table 3 (p. 5) says once or twice only. Suggested page 'pp. 2–3, 5' and wording '(Methods 2.2, p. 2; Table 3, p. 5) ... (Results 3.1, p. 3)'.
p. 5, 3.4, 1st sentence; Table 3 shows odds ratios only.
p. 6: 'Role of funding source: None' against the acknowledged HRC programme grant 16/600.

risk_of_bias.note: ROBINS-E matches the design. Overall high agreed: ROBINS-E allows high when concerns in several domains together substantially lower confidence, and here same-period reporting (reverse order possible), no adjustment for other illicit drug use or drug-market involvement, and correlated self-report all bear on an estimate whose lower limits are 1.00–1.04. One domain differs (below); it does not change the overall.

risk_of_bias_domains.note: Adjustment for possible mediators (psychotic symptoms, depression) in Model 2 is rightly noted as biasing towards no association.

The card itself calls such interventions probably uncommon in this general-population cohort, and nothing suggests they differ by exposure in a way that would move the same-period association; 'some concerns' here adds a domain without a mechanism.
The unreported pairwise tests between frequency categories (2.7) and the abstract's comparison with less frequent use support this rating.

interpretation_gap.note: Substantial agreed. The abstract's claim that weekly use carried higher odds than less frequent use (p. 1) is not backed by any reported comparison, and the Discussion's statement that the associations are not fully accounted for by antisocial personality and concurrent use of other substances (p. 5) overstates the adjustment set (alcohol and cannabis use disorders only; conduct problems only in childhood and adolescence).

missed: The dose-response analysis is not period-matched (Methods 2.7, 3rd paragraph, p. 3): it relates the heaviest frequency reported in any period to violence at any time from 18 to 35, so the heaviest use and the violence need not fall in the same period or in that order. With adjustment for a reduced set of fixed confounders only (3.4, p. 5), the gradient therefore says nothing about temporal order and is more open to confounding than the GEE models; this matters for whether a dose-response upgrade is considered.

Table 3 note a says the dose-response models are adjusted for the Table 2 Model 1 factors, while 2.7 and 3.4 say only those factors significant in Model 1 were used (seven listed in 3.4); text and note disagree. The card's analysis.covariates gives the reduced set, which is the better-supported reading.
